lesson.title: Two Ends of a Spectrum: Fast Reproducers and Efficient Competitors
lesson.summary: r-selected species are adapted to reproduce rapidly with many, low-investment offspring, often in unstable environments, while K-selected species are adapted to compete efficiently near carrying capacity with few, high-investment offspring; real species fall along a continuum between these two extremes rather than into strict categories.
lesson.body:
The letters r and K should look familiar: they are the same two parameters from the logistic growth equation, dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K), the intrinsic growth rate and the carrying capacity. r-selection and K-selection theory, first proposed by ecologists in the 1960s as an extension of that same framework, describes two contrasting sets of life history traits named for which of those two parameters a species' evolutionary strategy seems built around maximizing.

Species described as r-selected are built around maximizing r, the rate of increase. Their traits typically include rapid reproduction, large numbers of offspring per reproductive event, small body size, early sexual maturity, little or no parental care, and comparatively short lifespans. These traits tend to be favored in unstable, unpredictable, or frequently disturbed environments, where a population is often kept well below carrying capacity by density-independent disturbances such as harsh weather, so the ability to reproduce quickly and colonize newly available habitat matters more than competitive efficiency. Many insects, weedy annual plants, and bacteria are commonly cited examples.

Species described as K-selected are built around thriving near K, the carrying capacity. Their traits typically include slower reproduction, fewer offspring per event, larger body size, later sexual maturity, substantial parental investment, and longer lifespans. These traits tend to be favored in relatively stable environments where populations spend most of their time close to carrying capacity, so density-dependent competition for limited resources, rather than unpredictable disturbance, is the main challenge to survival and reproduction. Elephants, great apes, whales, and many long-lived trees are commonly cited examples.

A concrete plant comparison helps make the contrast tangible. Dandelions behave in a strongly r-selected way: they produce large numbers of small, wind-dispersed seeds that let them rapidly colonize newly disturbed ground, such as a bare patch of soil, with relatively little investment in any individual seed. Oak trees behave in a strongly K-selected way: they produce comparatively few, large, energy-rich acorns, each with enough stored resources to give a seedling a meaningfully better chance of establishing itself in an already crowded, resource-limited forest floor.

It is essential to treat r-selection and K-selection as describing a spectrum rather than a strict either-or classification. Very few species sit at either pure extreme, and most combine some traits associated with each end depending on which specific aspect of their life history is being considered. Many ecologists today also view the original r and K framework as a useful starting simplification that has since been refined by more detailed life history theory, since it does not capture every pattern seen across the diversity of real species, some large, slow-reproducing species live in fairly unstable environments, for instance, which does not fit the classic picture cleanly. Even with those caveats, thinking in terms of the r-K spectrum remains a helpful first lens for predicting how a species is likely to respond to a changing environment, and it draws directly on both life history strategies and carrying capacity from the two preceding chapters.
